We propose an unsupervised, end-to-end speech synthesis approach that addresses the necessity for high-quality speech without extensive, labeled data. By leveraging a large amount of text-aligned audio, the model generates speech automatically. To improve naturalness, the encoder employs sequences of transformations, transforming speech from one speaker to another and adjusting its timbre accordingly. Additionally, a supervisory module, consisting of a sequence-to-sequence module and a discriminator, aids the model by simulating the effects of acoustic encoding and decoding. This approach was tested on the 2018 Challenge of the Luedwig University Speech Challenge, and results confirm that it excels over comparable systems, particularly when evaluated under constrained conditions. Notably, our model achieves superior performance using approximately one-fifth the training data of a comparable model.

This study focuses on both the average and dynamic aspects of holographic dark energy within a sub-UV infrared irremissible context. By assuming a holographic dark energy model with complex forms and its essence under these conditions, we determine that these models behave as stable systems. Furthermore, using the thermodynamic first law in the context of Friedmann equations reveals that models behave like phantom-like models and cause a universe expansion at an accelerating rate. It also indicates that the evolution of this energy changes from a deceleration to an acceleration phase. Additionally, we conducted an observational study using the Hubble parameter data and found that our models' parameters fall within a specific range.

Multi-objective optimization in mixed integer non-linear problems (MOMILONP) poses significant challenges in solving, particularly in determining optimal solutions for complex real-world applications. To address this issue, researchers have proposed a multi-objective algorithm combining non-dominated sorting genetic method II and branch-and-bound, called MABBO-NSGAII. By leveraging the branch-and-bound technique, MABBO-PO-NSGAII seeks to outperform the pure branch-and-bound branch-and-bound-Pareo envelope method, known as BBO-PE, in solving MOMILONP problems. MABBO-NSGAII-BC achieves a balance between solution diversity through evolution-based genetic diversity and optimality through branch-and-bound, ultimately enhancing the quality and computational time of the solution near the Pareto front compared to BBO-PE.

We refine the concepts of internal completeness and integral completeness for Lie groups within synthetic differential geometry, then demonstrate their equivalence when the Lie group is connected. Moreover, we reinterpret these ideas in terms of solvability for their associated Lie algebras.

The amount of secure clinical data available is currently underutilized. By leveraging proven cyberinfrastructure technology that enables data providers to control access and release, doctors and researchers can efficiently search, locate, and collaboratively work on specific patient cases. This paper outlines a methodology to create a secure data sharing environment where researchers and clinicians can query and use specific data sets under the supervision of the data providers.

To improve aspect-based sentiment analysis, we've proposed a new approach called EMoSA, which uses a pre-trained language model called BERT to capture sentiment information about specific aspects, incorporating both the sentiment of the aspect itself and its context within reviews from similar products. By contrastive learning, our approach effectively extracts implicit emotion patterns that conventional methods struggle with, even for reviews with the same sentiment. Through experiments conducted both online and offline, our results demonstrate that the sentiment representations learned by EMoSA significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods. Our research and code are openly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/lemon96/EMoSA-ABSA.

We investigate the effects of binary covariates on medium level factors in case-control studies with binary outcomes. Our analysis reveals that traditional methods fail to accurately estimate these effects even under ideal conditions when using case-control samples, despite no bias being introduced. However, a precise formula allows us to determine the required population distribution for making these effects estimates, facilitating their calculation in various study designs, including matched case-control samples. Through simulation, we demonstrate the performance of these effects under different confounding levels and in the presence or absence of effect homogeneity among subgroups.

This study investigates secure communication systems for multiple users utilizing reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, which are now integral to next-generation networks, thereby enhancing both capacity and security in harsh environments. The proposed research considers the effects of hardware limitations during non-orthogonal multiaccess transmission, which can significantly impact the performance of modern communication networks. The study minimizes the maximum mean square error among multiple users by optimizing a two-stage beamforming strategy, which involves separate phase shift and power allocation. A novel performance analysis is provided, which reveals the system's achievable rates and reveals the benefits of perfect intelligence-assisted communication. The results indicate that intelligent surfaces can enable unique working rates, which are not possible in traditional networks. The simulation results also demonstrate the system's robustness against hardware impairments, highlighting the importance of considering this factor in practical network design. The simulation demonstrates that intelligent surfaces can bring the system's performance closer to its fully intelligent limit, thereby reducing the gap between practical and ideal performance.

We introduce a contrast-based strategy called a contrastive value strategy to improve executive function learning through observation, specifically focusing on resampling and relabeling perceptions. Building on this, we develop a hindsight summarization approach called HESUMMA to streamline the learning process and reduce the need for multiple trial runs. In addition, we present a theoretical contrastive value function framework that allows for the discovery of contrast-based rules with unlimited complexity. Furthermore, we incorporate HESUMMA into an existing framework called rules-based summary value function learning, called RSVF-L, to optimize the function's search for the most effective contrast-based rules. The proposed method, HESUMMA-RSVF, significantly outperforms other benchmark techniques in managing a diverse range of filtering and ranking tasks.

Investigations of solar breeze and substorm energy fluxes in the near-Earth environment can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms driving middle to inner heliosphere energy transport. Although the specific mechanisms remain unclear, understanding how the solar system responds to varying levels of solar activity is crucial. The Parker Solar Probe mission to the inner heliosphere has the potential to reveal new information about these energy transport mechanisms. We analyzed four energy flux observations from Parker Solar Probe, which included one encounter where a shock formed within 10 solar radii and another where the energy flux was dominated by a shock-induced event occurring 14.3 solar radii from the Sun. In contrast, we also examined encounter E21 where four distinct energetic particle events occurred, indicating that the interplanetary space at 18.5-26.5 solar radii is not in geospace-like state, but rather behaves like a different and distinct environment.

We have established a principal bundle with noncommutative fibers, its base, its holonomy C*-algebra, a universal counting C*-algebra for orbits, and its holonomy group acting on this algebra, along with a notion of horizontal orbit sections. Given a C*-algebra A, a locally compact space X, and a universal counting C*-algebra H for orbits, we have established a one-to-one correspondence between a triple (A, ξ, X) forming a principal G-bundle over X with a horizontal orbit section s, and based on s, a triple (A_s, ξ_s, H) forming a noncommutative principal bundle, its bundle, and its counting algebra, and also between triples (A, H, s) and (A_s, H, s). Additionally, our results demonstrate that any noncommutative principal bundle is isomorphic to a partial equivariant crossed product C*-algebra, its base is isomorphic to a universal counting C*-algebra for its total space, and its total space is isomorphic to a universal counting C*-algebra for its base.

Two cardinal characteristics, $u$ and $n_d$, are introduced and studied, both falling between $\aleph_1$ and the continuum. The $u$ cardinal is a variant of the uniformity of the ideal of measure zero sets, while $n_d$ is a modification of the bounding number. The distribution of $n_d$ relative to other cardinal characteristics is examined, and a factorization theorem for $n_d$ is proven. The factorization of $n_d$ implies that if the continuum is significantly larger than $2^{\mathfrak{p}}$, then $n_d$ equals the bounding number. The factorization also leads to the conclusion that $n_d$ equals the bounding number under certain conditions, such as when $\mathfrak{b}$ is less than or equal to $n_d$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ is less than or equal to the covering number of the bounding number. This investigation focuses on observing the phenomenon of fast and slow light within the context of a one-dimensional Heisenberg algebra modified by a $q$-deformation in an optomechanical system. We investigate how varying the deformation parameter $q$ influences the coefficients associated with optical mode propagation velocity and clarity. The $q$-deformation is found to control both the group velocity and clarity of light, with its effects varying based on the order of the mechanical operator involved. Furthermore, our study reveals that the $q$-deformation can induce blue- and red-shifted peaks, and that the system's conditions are capable of enhancing the slow light effect and increasing the area under these peaks.

In the context of nuclear spectroscopy, the presence of negative relative sigma bands in the dynamical group model indicates R-group failure, which is associated with the absence of specific symmetries that should be observable in experiments, particularly in the realm of adverse hadron-antihadron systems, such as antiprotonic atoms and pions-nuclei interactions. Within the Two-Rotors Model for baryon octets, the occurrence of adverse R-parity scissors modes can be identified through a unique energy spectrum pattern that features a massive, negative relative sigma band, alongside a positive one. Notably, the modes adverse to R-parity involve the interaction of two rotors, one representing a nucleon and the other a light antiquark cluster, within the framework of a reflective symmetry plane.

A new cell-mean based neural network method is developed to solve hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations in this work. The method utilizes a novel, unstructured cell-averaging approach for input and, combined with neural networks, enables the interpolation of unknown variables at specific points within cells. This method requires no mesh, is free from a Courant-Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy restriction, and is free from dispersion or oscillation. As a result, it is well-suited for solving discontinuous PDEs. We test this method on hyperbolic PDEs at a cell level and extend it to parabolic and diffusion equations by adding an implicit time-stepping scheme. We provide several numerical examples to validate the method's effectiveness in solving PDEs with shocks, contact discontinuities, and boundary layers.

The ALICE collaboration is focused on studying heavy-ion collisions in detail, particularly concerning hadron-hadron, electron-electron and electron-nucleus interactions at the CERN LHC. The experiment, comprising hadronic detectors, muon spectrometers, and TPCs, will be significantly upgraded with the introduction of a new electromagnetic calorimeter, upgraded muon spectrometers, and TPC readout systems, in order to enhance the capabilities for the studies to be conducted beyond LHC Run 3.

The Unruh effect describes how an accelerating observer perceives a Minkowski vacuum as a thermal state due to acceleration, causing a separation of pure and entangled states. Our research reveals that the Unruh effect also induces entanglement between the left and right Rindler wedges when considering the past light cones of such states. We've also developed a geometric approach to calculating the Unruh-Berry phase by examining the entanglement between the future and past light cones, which remains constant under classical Riemannian transformations. This new phase, in conjunction with the Unruh-Conway phase, forms the Unruh total geometric phase, enabling the detection of timelike Unruh phenomena through changes in its value.

A significant challenge in IT service management is the process of Incident Response where existing tools often struggle to keep up with escalating demands. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Multilingual Event Extraction framework designed to enhance automated incident response by using large language models to identify and organize natural language descriptions of key incident components. We have compiled a diverse dataset consisting of over 5,000 incident descriptions in 11 languages to support research in various NLP tasks, and upon evaluating our results, found that not only does this framework excel at extracting and structuring incidents in multilingual contexts, but it also outperforms comparable datasets in English. This research is being made available to the public to promote open-source development and collaboration.

We derive new global characteristics for vector bundles over complete metric spaces by integrating local inclusions into a global framework, which enables a more in-depth understanding of characteristic forms of vector bundles in relation to their geometric properties. This approach also provides a general context for existing pointwise push-forward formulae, including those by Segre, Chern, Wu, Chern-Moser, Newstead, Newstead-Wall, and Simons. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the positivity of characteristic forms on a vector bundle and the curvature properties of the underlying manifold.

Our analysis examines the impact of the stellar wind on the X-ray timing properties of an accreting black hole, specifically in the system Cyg X-1 during its hard state. We utilized a multi-instrument approach, combining XMM-NN and INTEGRAL observations to create a comprehensive model of the system. We established that the stellar wind is the primary source of the wind's motion, as evidenced by the flat dispersion measure profile and the wind's constant velocity, allowing us to calculate the space velocity of the wind's source. Furthermore, we investigated the effect of the wind on the black hole's X-ray emission using two distinct models. We found a significant positive correlation between the wind's density and the black hole's X-ray emission across the energy spectrum in the 2-124 keV range. Furthermore, we established that the system's phase lag spectrum is unaffected by the wind, as it is consistent with the black hole's disk-line emission model. We also established that the system's QPO properties are not influenced by the wind, as it is consistent with the presence of a wind-induced hard X-ray background. Our findings indicate that the wind and the black hole's X-ray emission are not interconnected in a complex manner.

The study of a specific ether-like modification of N=1 super-Yang-Mills theory is conducted within a thermal environment, with significant implications for quark-gluon plasma dynamics. By super-Yang-Mannis-mons-formulating this correction, researchers discovered it's directly related to the Euler density of a 4D spacetime when analyzed in classical terms. Consequently, the authors have derived the perturbation equations and computed the temperature-dependent correction to black hole solutions, leading to the derivation of the correction to the Hamiltonian and the study of its impact on thermal averages of various gauge invariant properties.

Our concurrent parsing approach achieves high accuracy on a broad range of languages by leveraging the strengths of both types of analyses, allowing for the parsing of ambiguous constructions that are difficult for traditional methods to handle. This efficiency is further enhanced by our parallel algorithm, which makes the combined learning process feasible. The benefits of our approach are demonstrated through a detailed evaluation on the 2018 CTB 5 multilingual treebank dataset.

We conducted simulations of magnetized postmerger disk outflows following a neutron star neutron star merger, where the dynamo-generated magnetic field in the accretion disk significantly influences outflow properties. By artificially amplifying the disk's magnetic field, we observed the effect of magnetic forces on outflow properties. Our results indicate that the effect of the dynamo-generated magnetic field in these mergers is negligible compared to the effect of manually amplifying the disk's magnetic field by a factor of ten. In these simulations, the annular region of the disk experiences rapid rotation and develops strong bar modes, resulting in amplified magnetic fields that influence the outflow. The orientation of the jet axis correlates with the direction of the helical bar mode, and as a result, the footprints of the bar pattern dictate the orientation of the jet axis. The jet-driven wind shows signs of being driven by magnetic forces in the disk region, and its speed and mass outflow rate increase by an order of magnitude. The outcome of the simulation suggests significant anisotropies in the wind structure, and our results indicate that the jet-driven wind could power kilonova emission, potentially contributing to blue or double-humped peaks in the light curves.

Our analysis of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Early Type Galaxy Survey reveals significant findings regarding early-type galaxies with masses greater than $10^{10} M_{\odot}$. In these galaxies, we discovered that tidal features account for approximately 10-20% of the flux, indicating that they are more prevalent and complex than previously believed. Based on cross-correlation studies with optical and radio galaxies, we found that early-type galaxies exhibit tidal features consistent with both major and minor merger origins, with minor mergers being more prevalent than previously assumed. These results challenge the traditional perception of early-type galaxies as static systems, instead suggesting that they are dynamically active and evolving. Furthermore, we found that early-type galaxies with tidal features are more abundant and massive than featureless galaxies, a discovery that highlights the importance of including tidal feature galaxies in understanding galaxy evolution.

Building on the azimuthally symmetric gravitational theory, which posits that gravity repels rather than attracts, researchers have suggested that such a concept can effectively explain various phenomena in the universe at an early stage. In such a framework, the development of rotating celestial bodies and their associated gaseous and stellar distributions occurs through a process of vertical collapse, driven by a central singularity. In the early stages of these distributions, the growth is facilitated by bipolar outflows in the polar direction, which are accompanied by rotational expansion in the equatorial direction. As a result, the three-dimensional distribution of matter takes the shape of a galactic disk, which is further shaped by the continuous expansion of its components in the equatorial direction, ultimately leading to spiral galaxies.

We have studied the M81 group galaxy with the Very Large Array for 11 candidates of Fast Radio Bursts, including one confirmed event, located at 1.6 gigahertz. Our research found that none of the other ten sources showed any optical connection, setting a new limit on their brightness at 25.1 magnitude, with the potential to find a companion star every 10 years. Based on our findings, we estimate a maximum of 3.1 companion stars with the potential to be detected at 25.1 magnitude or less, with the probability of detection being 50% or less. We have derived a stricter upper limit on the rate of hydrogen lines from our null results, which is about 10^-4, with the probability of detection being 50% or less. Our findings suggest that binary systems of neutron stars are unlikely to have low-mass companions and delay their merger for more than 10 million years. Our research supports the idea that low-mass companions are unlikely to be a common source of repeating millisecond pulsators, with the probability of detection being 50% or less. Our findings also suggest a lower limit on the age of the neutron star merger event, which could potentially challenge the 50% probability hypothesis, by setting a limit on the delay time of 10 million years or less.

High-power laser technology finds diverse applications in inertial fusion energy, precision manufacturing, particle beam acceleration, and next-generation lighting solutions like LED and OLED, necessitating advanced design and reverse engineering capabilities for high-performance laser components and materials. This review encompasses current developments in computer-aided design and reverse engineering tools for various high-power laser applications, including tailored beam profiles, random phase modulators, non-linear materials, and multi-objective optimization techniques for metal processing.

When generating text, it's often necessary to consider multiple possibilities and make decisions on visual cues. We've developed a novel approach by integrating a backpointer key into keyboard layouts, enabling writers to leverage visual controls as needed. Through controlled experiments, we investigated the impact of this integration on a diverse range of participants, both in academic and everyday writing contexts. Notably, our results showed that a small subset of participants consistently utilized visual controls when composing text, suggesting that a more widespread acceptance of visual controls may have been overlooked in text generation research.

To enhance transaction privacy, the adoption of cryptocurrency transactions involving RingCT is recommended. Although ring mix facilitates ring transactions, the verification process is particularly time-consuming, making it unsuitable for adoption within the Tezos blockchain. In an effort to address this issue, the Delegated RingCT protocol has been developed to accelerate ring mix transactions. By incorporating an additional signed transaction, the Delegated RingCT protocol enables ring mix to accept existing accounts rather than requiring new ones, thus improving its scalability and reducing processing times. In addition, the Delegated RingCT protocol maintains a high level of privacy and is currently being tested for integration into Tezblock, a Tezos-based testing network.

Scanning a bright particle physics beam in the transverse plane by altering its angle is a widely used diagnostic technique in both fixed and variable annihilation experiments. By analyzing how the beam's intensity changes laterally, users can infer crucial parameters such as the separation and orientation of the beam's components as well as its overall spread. Furthermore, making two-dimensional angle-based measurements provides an even more comprehensive understanding of the beam's behavior.

This research proposes a collaborative data-driven approach to resolve the fundamental challenge of parameter identification in complex models using limited data and uncertain data sources. In a collaborative framework, multiple systems with shared parameters and distinct data sets can exchange information to optimize their respective parameter sets for improved performance and accuracy. A specific application of interest involves identifying parameters for a particular class of reaction networks, particularly those with parameters that are both shared and unique, and are often obscured by noise. A specific example, a 2-parameter generalization of the well-known Schl\"{o}gl model with two reaction channels, is used to demonstrate the need for collaboration in sharing information. A specific optimization algorithm is used to solve the problem of estimating the parameters for both individual and collaborative settings, and is applied to simulate noisy data generated from the Schl\"{o}gl model. In collaborative settings, the initial parameter estimates for each participant are used to solve the problem independently and collaboratively, respectively, and the results indicate that the collaborative approach significantly improves the accuracy of the estimated parameters, with an error of less than 0.01, compared to a maximum of 0.21 in the non-collaborative setting.

This research proposes that the recently discovered narrow resonance $\Upsilon(10753)$ is actually a hybrid molecule composed of $\Upsilon(10610)$ and $\pi^+\pi^-$. To confirm this, the study further argues that the decay channels of $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ ($n$=1,2,...) are triggered via a loop mechanism involving the exchange of two pions ($\pi^+\pi^-$). Consequently, detailed calculations of the ratio between the decay widths of $\Upsilon(10753)$ decaying into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ were conducted using an effective Lagrangian approach. Ultimately, theoretical branching ratios for the decay of $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ ($n$=1,2,...) were obtained and their validity tested against the data collected by the BESIII experiment.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique, quantized optimization with interval-restricted askew stochastic gradient descent (AskewSGD), designed to train fully quantized deep neural networks (DNNs) to network size independent precision (NSIP) levels of accuracy DNNs can achieve to their full precision. Our method, based on the QNNO framework, quantizes every parameter and optimization variable in DNNs to a fixed-precision codebook and trains the parameterized optimization variables rather than the weights and biases as typically done. An key innovation involved in QNNO is the incorporation of a non-standard, asymmetric stochastic gradient estimator formulated under an entropic regularized optimal transport problem constrained by a maximum entropy distribution. Our annealed optimization method relaxes constraints gradually and combines it with a fixed-precision training scheme that enforces restricted interval constraints on all parameters through the addition of interval constraints on the estimator in iterative updates. Our approach was tested on image classification tasks with various network architectures, and it consistently achieved network size independent precision levels of accuracy DNNs can achieve to their full precision through automatic differentiation, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

The utilization of soft robotics has gained significant attention in 4IR research due to its inherent versatility and adaptability. Implementing precise control strategies for these systems remains a significant challenge, primarily because of the complex dynamics of the materials themselves, the absence of well-documented mathematical models, and the substantial distortions that occur during actuation. Research into controlling soft robots is divided into two primary categories: model-based and model-free. Model-based approaches, which are the focus of this analysis, involve utilizing mathematical descriptions to establish the relationship between input forces and resulting deformations. These methods can be categorized further into three main types: employing constitutive equations, modeling physical phenomena, and utilizing neural networks. Our objective in this paper is to provide an exhaustive review of these model-based strategies, highlighting their advantages, limitations, and future prospects.

This study delves into the properties of a specific subset within the $n \times n$ invertible matrix set, which preserves a norm-defined condition across all indices. This subset serves as a variant of the generalized orthogonal group, a condition that reduces to a familiar form under specific conditions. Focusing particularly on the case where $n = 2$, we derive various characteristics and establish their extensions to higher dimensions. A notable finding demonstrates that this variant of the Jacobi group can be equivalently characterized as another norm-defined condition, which may contain the generalized pro-orthogonal group at its center. We also establish relationships between this subset and the pro-orthogonal group through explicit formula representations for matrix group elements, also for the case where the condition is replaced with a generalized pro-unitary group, providing formulas for matrix in both these scenarios.

The challenge of fact verification in tables involves checking if a given statement accurately reflects the information within a table. Researchers have made progress in this area, with existing models performing competitively. However, these models have a major weakness: they're prone to errors if the table's structure is incorrect, misinterpreted or if irrelevant information is included in the associated passage. Our study, with a new exploration of table fact verification, seeks to address these issues. We have created a new dataset, characterized by complex tables and intricate relationships between these structures and the sentences. Our dataset allows for three different types of questions: (i) verifying the accuracy of an assertion using the full table, (i) verifying the accuracy of an assertion using a subset of the table, and (ii) verifying the accuracy of an assertion to determine if an extraction of information from the table to an assertion is necessary. Our results indicate that existing models struggle to solve these sub-tasks, and we have developed an approach, called Exploring Disassembly (EDIS), which significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on our dataset by correctly identifying whether the full table is necessary, partial tables are necessary, or the assertion can be verified by extracting information from the assertion.

Our method introduces an innovative generator for conditional generative adversarial networks (CGAN), decoupling the condition from its visible presentation to preserve the topological integrity of the underlying data space. The generator integrates a random forest structure, which not only maps conditions into a high-dimensional space but also enables interpolation between different conditions. As a result, the interpolations performed by the generator accurately reflect the underlying data space structure. Due to the efficiency of its design, the generator is well-suited for CGAN, allowing for the training of more realistic models without overfitting. We showcase the effectiveness of the proposed method on the task of image imputation in a medical context, achieving the best performance in terms of both model performance and training speed, as verified through experiments on the MNIST, CT-MAMMD, and Patchwork UCI datasets.

The nested sampling algorithm is an efficient method for Bayesian inference that effectively balances acceptance rates and profile likelihoods during optimization. Its performance is influenced by the step selector used, yet research into this aspect has been limited. In this study, we examine five step selectors: uniform, adaptive, floor, ceiling, and geometric. Through our analysis, we found that the choice of step selector has minimal impact on marginal likelihood estimates and acceptance rates, but it does affect runtime significantly. Consequently, we recommend using the adaptive selector due to its ability to reduce computation costs without compromising accuracy, outperforming uniform, floor, and ceiling selectors, and also showing differences from the geometric selector.

For certain graph classes like trees and 3-convex graphs, we can efficiently store distance information within a 1 x factor of accuracy using 1st O(log n) bits per vertex. However, distance labeling for general graphs remains unresolved, even with an arbitrarily large labeling factor, with the best results so far being an O(log n) bits solution requiring 6 polynomial in n errors. In a significant breakthrough, we propose a novel solution to this problem, specifically for planar graphs. Our graph labeling scheme achieves a 2 x distance accuracy with a significant reduction in errors to 1st O(log n) bits, specifically 4 potential errors. In the event of vertex corruption, we can also efficiently identify faulty vertices in an O(log^2 n) time. Notably, we prove that an O(log n) bits solution with only 4 potential errors is impossible, thus highlighting the optimality of our proposed solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that we can achieve constant errors for nearly all graph classes by sacrificing one bit, specifically for planar graphs, we can reduce the errors to merely 1.

In the thermodynamic limit of Bose-Hubbard models with site-imposed chaos and subjected to external forces and dissipation, the dynamical generation of correlations is explored within the Bogoliubov many-body framework. Our analysis reveals two distinct mechanisms for correlation generation: the rapid creation of correlations shared by all modes within the system's real-frequency bandwidth upon sudden changes in parameters, and the emergence of correlations generated through time-domain coupling within the system's real-frequency support when parameters are slowly and continuously modulated. In contrast, correlation patterns produced by imaginary-frequency support remain unchanged due to the specific form of coupling. In terms of wavevector space, this results in anti-diagonal correlation structures, revealing the distinct influence of forcing and dissipation within different regions of wavevector space.

This research focuses on solving an elliptic equation in a form involving
divergence that arises from the principles of general relativity and plasma
dynamics. Specifically, a given current $f$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^N$,
belonging to a space where the square of a function with compact support is
measurable, is considered. A challenge arises of finding a weak solution $u$
to the equation $-\mathrm{div}(A(x)\nabla u) = \mathrm{div}(f)$ within a
domain, with a given boundary condition where $u$ approaches zero. A novel
approach is introduced by defining a space of functions where the derivative
of the function, when added to the gradient of the function, belongs to a space
where the square of the function with compact support is measurable, along with
a finite energy space. By applying techniques including monotone convergence
convergence and compactness, existence, uniqueness of solutions, and a
regularity estimate are demonstrated. Additionally, conditions for
regularity of the function $u$ in terms of the given current $f$ are
established.

Recent advancements in Out-of-Distribution detection using Out-of-Distribution stratification have primarily relied on a complex and time-consuming approach, which limits their scalability. In contrast, we present a novel method that integrates Gaussian Processes to approximate the stratification without requiring the use of the black-box model. This method, ODS-GP, leverages the properties of Distributional Gaussian Processes to approximate the output distribution of black-box deep neural networks. By leveraging these properties, we develop an efficient approach to perform out-of-distribution detection across multiple classes. Our method can handle both generative and discriminative models, as well as correlated and non-correlated outputs. In our experiments, we found ODS-GP to be more accurate than existing baselines, particularly in scenarios involving correlated outputs, and to operate effectively at low computation costs.

In theory, a Bose-Einstein condensate can exist independently of temperature within non-integrable quantum systems, but in practice, it is disrupted by thermal effects. Our research reveals that, despite the widespread assumption that thermal effects invariably destroy Bose condensation, it can sometimes be protected by isolating the system in a specific state, even under intense thermal disruption. We have experimentally identified a specific configuration in the Az2 chain model - an open-chain arrangement surrounded by a periodic lattice - where such state isolation occurs naturally, leading to stable Bose condensation even in the presence of significant thermal disruption, an outcome that contrasts sharply with the effects of similar but distinct Floquet HE dynamics.

We provide details for an enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle, specifically for the H\"older continuity of $C^2$ functions with bounded second derivatives, in the solution to the Monge-Ampere equation. Our approach involves a combination of elementary techniques and refined H\"older estimates for eigenvalues in the matrix of the Hessian of the distance function. As a result, we can relax the right-hand side (right-hand side) Harnack inequality, maintaining H\"older continuity for the solution. In particular, we can demonstrate H\"older continuity for the solution to the Monge-Ampere equation without assuming the right-hand side is bounded, provided H\"older continuity for the Hessian of the distance function is established.

Statistical methods are used to evaluate the long-term stability of complex clock signals that fluctuate in an unpredictable manner. This new analysis technique is specifically designed for a type of optical clock that combines high precision with a compounding effect of errors over time, making it suitable for applications like geodesic monitoring and relativistic studies. However, existing analysis tools struggle to handle this type of signal due to their focus on short-term and medium-term fluctuations. Here, we introduce and test different methods that effectively analyze long-term optical clock signals, analyzing real data from an advanced Yb lattice clock and comparing it with historical data from a Sr lattice clock over a ten-year period.

In Service Function Chain (SFC)-based Software Defined Networking (SDN), maintaining high availability and reliability is highly critical. The increasing demand for real-time SFC applications, along with the potential for failures in fog nodes and faults in traffic paths, significantly complicates network operations. Therefore, the goal of our proposed fog-supported, energy-efficient, joint SFC approach is to ensure optimal resource management, fault mitigation, and failure recovery while operating within the constraints of fog-enabled nodes for real-time services. A centralized, optimization-based solution is employed to address this problem, with energy efficiency as a primary consideration. A Distributed Quotient Backpressure (DQB) algorithm is used to address the nonconvexity of Linear Programming (LP) formulations, resulting in a time complexity of O(T(γ+β)F). Simulation results demonstrate that our solution effectively meets real-time latency requirements and significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms. Furthermore, numerical outcomes validate the justifications for prevention and restoration mechanisms within real-time SFC contexts, highlighting their necessity to minimize service disruptions.

A loss function's role in loss minimization optimization problems is crucial, yet its effects on gradient descent are complex. Introducing a new approach using "gradient surgery," researchers can examine how a loss function works by separating it into a score and odds components. By iteratively using the best possible score component, they can find the best loss functions for a given optimization task. The method has been tested and demonstrates potential as a systematic way to design effective loss functions. The analysis also provides insights into loss function structure and offers a criterion for comparing different designs. The method's code is available in the PyTorch framework with minimal dependencies.

A novel class of holographic error correction codes, called hyper-invariant MERA (iMERA), is proposed. These codes, inspired by the dynamics of quantum quenches in quantum field theories, exhibit properties of diffeomorphism invariant holographic descriptions. By leveraging the MERA circuit's intrinsic symmetries, our iMERA construction achieves a dual power-law entanglement entropy behavior, incorporates a long-range algebraic correlation and implements a quantum erasure code capable of correcting local errors. These codes are realized within the framework of a free boson conformal field theory, enabling explicit computation of code parameters and error correction capabilities. Our results establish iMERA as a highly efficient and scalable quantum erasure code, emphasizing the value of symmetries for robust quantum information processing.

The Galactic Center's population of dense filamentary structures, observed through K-band imaging by the SOAR telescope, has been analyzed through KSPAWM, a tool that separates filamentary structures from background noise. A KSWMF catalog, consisting of 1,030 filaments, was created and compared in terms of spatial distribution. This was done by examining the distances between filaments (DF) and stars within the Galactic Center, using KSWMF measurements and accounting for the varying transparency of the line-of-sight. A distribution function for D, F, and D, S was calculated and analyzed using statistical parameters such as the median, quartiles, and skewness. These statistics show that filaments are located between each other with a skewness of 0.924, indicating a non-uniform distribution. This was further confirmed by comparing filament-fragment spacing with median star spacing in 2D and 1D projections, which showed that filaments are not uniformly distributed. This led to a hypothesis that filaments in the Galactic Center exhibit a level of clustering, which could be attributed to non-gravitational effects.

A new method for the Grid-Forming Inverter (GFI) to contribute to grid stability during power outages is introduced, conserving energy by simultaneously decreasing the voltage and increasing the power factor. The proposed conservation voltage decrease control strategy is defined as follows: (i) the GFI will adjust its voltage negatively and increase the power factor when the distribution network reduces its voltage; (ii) this control strategy is designed to be effective even when the GFI has a limited capacity. The proposed control approach involves the GFI's local monitoring of voltage violations and adjusting its output accordingly. Our analysis confirms that this control strategy results in a uniform reduction of the voltage across the distribution network, and we demonstrate through simulations that this method effectively conserves energy while maintaining stability.

In non-stochastic multi-armed bandits, we tackle issues involving delayed feedback and various interactive settings where an advisor, guided by external sources, recommends arms with potentially delayed advice also from non-stochastic sources. Notably, this work introduces a new class of advisors capable of adapting advice delay based on the arm being selected, presenting both technical obstacles and potential benefits in comparison to previous models. On one hand, this increased flexibility in advisor models can lead to decreased regret for the bandit in our setting, as we show that the optimal value of a specific "delay function" results in lower regret than scenarios without advisor input when it is present, which in turn can be viewed as a form of "free information". However, this improved value of the delay function also introduces new challenges in terms of developing strategies for the bandit to achieve competitive performance. In particular, this work introduces new regret bounds influenced by a specific set of parameters and demonstrates that this result is robust, offering improved results over models with constant advisor delay in cases where it is not.

Current dialogue systems still fall short of meeting human expectations for conversational capabilities, largely due to limitations in natural language generation. To address this, we developed LEATHER, an innovative framework that integrates local contextual understanding with long-term memory to create more engaging and coherent conversations. Our novel memory strategy, inspired by human learning processes, enables the system to adapt and improve over time by identifying knowledge gaps and seeking out relevant information from external sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that LEATHER not only creates text that is difficult to distinguish from human writing, but also exhibits increased conversational depth, coherence, and consistency over time.

This work examines an innovative Monte Carlo approach for simulating lattice QCD under the influence of temperature and quark density, which overcomes existing limitations by allowing the use of Wilson quark actions without incurring additional costs, while maintaining the benefits of a single Monte Carlo representation. The method showcases its efficacy by conducting simulations on lattice configurations generated at non-zero temperatures, thus offering insights into the impact of finite temperatures on these configurations. The study further includes a crucial verification step, verifying that the introduced stochastic sources do not adversely affect the convergence of Monte Carlo sampling.

To ensure the safety of offshore wind turbines, accurate stress predictions are crucial. This paper proposes a new method for predicting overall stress distributions within offshore wind turbine towers using data-driven modeling. By applying a sequential strategy to the Gaussian Process (GP) regression, the proposed approach effectively handles complex, high-dimensional neural network inputs. It begins by mapping the complex inputs to a simpler sequential space, and then applies the GP model to this space. The resulting predictive models are then combined to retrieve the original input space's GP models. The efficacy of the proposed method is validated through numerical examples. Furthermore, the paper showcases its application to a real-world problem involving the modeling of wind turbine tower stresses under varying sea states.

Social media platforms like Twitter facilitate the dissemination of information and ideas in real-time, significantly impacting the perception and analysis of the world. The increasing number of Twitter users enables close examination of events and their effects through their online activity patterns. This research investigates Twitter's utility by analyzing the distribution of messages related to a specific event, namely the Izmir earthquake. Our initial findings highlight how Twitter can effectively track public sentiment and engagement in response to critical events.

A group is classified as having the $R_\infty$ property when all its infinite cyclic twisted conjugate overgroups satisfy a specific condition, which can be characterized by the index of a particular ideal in reduced nilpotent residues. This ideal was introduced in the study and its results can be used to determine when groups formed by generalized Baumslag-Solitar group extensions exhibit the $R_\infty$ property in various nilpotent quotients. Furthermore, a new introduction method for these ideals can be applied, which has overgroups that can be characterized by the above mentioned index when formed by free products of infinite cyclic groups with finite twisted conjugacy classes.

A technique, known as time-mapping, is widely employed in physics and chemistry experiments to uncover hidden dynamics hidden within a system's behavior as it evolves over time. A widely used method leverages model parameters and initial conditions, which are optimized in relation to a system's governing equations, rather than directly in relation to measured data. Although initially conceived for continuous data, a key limitation of this technique arises when it is applied to discrete time-mapped data, typically obtained from stroboscopic measurements. Existing approaches either involve a heavy numerical cost or require highly accurate initial guesses, which may not always be feasible. In this work, a new, highly efficient algorithm is presented, based on optimizing the trajectory of the system in its intrinsic basis. This basis can be defined analytically for many standard dynamical models, such as those including the logistic map, pendulum, Kerr nonlinear oscillator, and Lorentz attractor. Through simulations, the proposed method is shown to be effective in recovering complex attractors and is resilient to noise. The presented technique is shown to be versatile, applicable to a variety of common measurement protocols.

Naturalistic driving studies are limited by insufficient data due to their intricate setup, which makes researchers turn to driven simulators. A newlyintroduced dataset, SceNDD, offers a vast repository of genuine driving scenarios collected from a high-fidelity simulator, covering a wide variety of scenarios not frequently encountered in real-world driving. Unlike traditional naturalistic data, SceNDD's scenarios are preselected, ensuring a balanced distribution. Each scenario is meticulously documented with detailed metadata. We conducted an evaluation of multiple behavior prediction models using SceNDD's spatial data and revealed the dataset's unique advantages in promoting novel research. Moreover, the dataset is made available for the research community to explore and build upon.

We investigate the reflected entropy in characterizations of entanglement phase transitions within conformal field models featuring boundary states and interfaces. Utilizing the extremal surface/conical defect method, we analyze the phase transitions in three distinct scenarios: the bulk/boundary ratio, the interface/ratio within the boundary, and the interface ratio. Furthermore, we derived a relationship between the cross ratio and the boundary block in the context of the boundary O(N) model, subsequently extending this relationship to the context of the interface in the same model.

Recent research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) is being explored to improve wireless communication systems by adapting their propagation characteristics. To achieve this adaptation, accurate RIS channel estimation is necessary, which typically relies on a hardware system with perfect transceivers. However, this requirement is impractical in real-world scenarios where transceiver hardware is not perfect. Furthermore, current approaches are highly susceptible to noise and multiplication errors caused by imperfect hardware, rendering them unsuitable for systems with limited cyclic prefix (CP). Therefore, our goal is to develop a precise and computationally efficient model-free nonlinear system identification method using an optimized Extended Learning Machine (ELM) to accurately estimate RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems with limited CP and imperfect hardware. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach even in scenarios with limited CP and imperfect hardware.

Nielsen and Chuang's standard measurement model is widely used in quantum computation, but a significant issue with it is that obtaining specific measurement outcomes may involve multiple projective operations. A novel variation theorem is introduced with a single energy-based measurement that guarantees achieving any desired outcome through a unitary evolution rather than projective operations. This unitary evolution can be constrained to operate over a limited subspace defined by the initial state and the target measurement state. The newly formulated theorem has been applied to address the quantum search problem, thereby eliminating the need for projective measurements.

We are currently exploring a class of Anti-de Sitter space solutions that originate from the 11-dimensional supergravity theory. These solutions are derived from specific 8-dimensional manifolds that possess a specific structure, as well as special connections that are G2-based. Our investigation centers on identifying Anti-de Sitter solution sources by identifying conditions that define flat sections in the curvature of these specialized connections. It is ultimately demonstrated that nearly G2 8-manifold solutions provide a generic example of such Anti-de Sitter sources.

This study's primary goal is to evaluate the data protection measures implemented in the Coronavirus-SUS COVID-19 contact tracing mobile application in Brazil. To achieve this, specific aspects of the system were investigated, including data encryption at rest and in transit, geolocation processing, data verification, data collection frequency, and data sharing protocols with health authorities. Notably, one crucial component, the homomorphic encryption protocol used for distance calculation between infected and exposed users, was not fully understood. Consequently, this paper presents a comprehensive overview of the system, including design and implementation details, with a particular focus on the secretariat's source code, which was publicly available.

Neural systems are thought to operate based on principles of digital circuitry, but these systems may incorporate and benefit from analog signals and components, which could include the advantages of genuine quantum phenomena. A review is provided of the properties of natural components found in biological systems, which could exhibit quantum behaviors, as well as potential signaling methods and processing strategies within these systems. Although there is still much to uncover about the existence of quantum effects in nature, existing discoveries reveal a remarkable intersection between biology and quantum physics. Additionally, the possibility that our understanding of these biological quantum phenomena in neural systems could inform the design of more effective artificial neural networks and quantum computing models cannot be dismissed.

This paper presents a novel tool, an ACL2 based C code generator that can translate ACL2 specifications into valid C code and produce certified C code in ACL2 format, after thorough analysis and verification of the implemented functionality.

A thorough analysis of the Iochroma family, a group of asteroids formed from a single collision, is conducted using z8 data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Irregular orbital variations in Iochroma are identified, indicating possible past dynamic events. Detailed orbital modeling places Iochroma at past resonances, including a 3:5 resonance, and highlights its irregular shape. These findings support the hypothesis that Iochroma's present shape is a result of structural relaxation after the collision that created the Iochroma family. Iochroma's behavior is compared with other members of the family, and the impact of light pressure on the group's dynamics is assessed.

Precise complex expressions for both the Hurwitz zeta functions and the generalized Bernoulli polynomials at specific integer points for the rational values of pi are derived from a unified method. Building upon H. W. Zhang's research, a formula relating Bernoulli polynomials and Ramanujan's zeta function is established. Subsequently, a modified equation involving the Hurwitz zeta function is formulated and connects the two functions. Multiple integral representations for the zeta function are obtained through the use of the Eisenstein series formula. Additionally, formulas for evaluating the Hessian function at both even and odd points are derived, complemented by relevant identities.

We establish that logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology with the presence of a mod 2 torsion element in the base, applied to complex projective spaces of a complex vector group $V$, is isomorphic to mod 2 field cohomology with the mod 3 cohomology with nilpotent loop space actions of a particular odd-dimensional sphere. Isomorphic to this is a specific kind of elliptic cohomology with loop space actions of $S^1 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$. Isomorphic to this is an module category of certain elliptic categories with loop space actions of a nilpotent sphere, whose homotopy category's elliptic cohomology with circle-equivariance, applied to projective space cohomologies of $S^1$-representation $S^1$-spaces $V$, holds a particular identity in which it is equal to a particular elliptic categories with nilpotent loop space actions of a particular odd-dimensional sphere $S^k$, $0\leq k<2$, whose homotopy category's elliptic cohomology with circle-equivariance, applied to the CP^q $q\geq 1$, holds a particular identity in which it is equal to a particular elliptic categories with nilpotent loop space actions of a particular odd-dimensional sphere $S^k$, $0\leq k<2$, whose homotopy category's elliptic cohomology.

We examine several machine learning models for topological data analysis, including their benefits and drawbacks, and highlight their applications in physics, particularly in the fields of statistical and quantum mechanics.  A prominent neural network model, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), is highlighted for its capacity to identify and process complex data patterns, which can be used to describe intricate systems and their properties in quantum physics and cosmology.  Key insights from our findings are that CNNs are well-suited for topology-preserving feature extraction, making them a valuable tool for physics research.

This paper undertends a comprehensive analysis of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production from $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions, exploring processes such as $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ where the center-of-mass energy is approximately 10.6 GeV. By utilizing the nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) factorization approach at next-to-leading order, we identify the two dominant production mechanisms, the $b$-quark box diagram and the $c$-quark triangle diagram, contributing to the $^3S_1^{[J/\psi]}+\eta_c$ process. We find that the $C$-quark triangle diagram significantly outweighs the $B$-quark box diagram in terms of magnitude and that the $s$-channel diagrams' contributions are negligible in comparison. Through detailed simulations of the angular distributions for $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$, we predict that the $C$-quark triangle diagram will produce an ellipticity exceeding 0.1 for $J/\psi$ at this energy, at least twice the length of the previous estimates obtained via the factorization approach at leading order.

This research focuses on the users' mental models of Signal encryption system's user-defined PINs. Through qualitative interviews, we discovered a lack of consensus among Signal users regarding the PIN's function, including its impact on user experience and data security. To address this ambiguity, we conducted a study on 30 Signal users to examine their satisfaction levels and mental understanding of the PIN system. We also investigated how users create and establish trust through signal users, and identified potential improvements to signal users' design, including user testing and research.

A groundbreaking technique for accurately and efficiently integrating solar energy into the complex optimization problems of a power system has been developed. The proposed method transforms solar-energy calculation into a quadrature problem, and uses a tailored Gaussian quadrature approach to minimize computational costs without compromising accuracy. The method is characterized by its adaptability and reliability, and can be directly applied to any location and time by relying solely on the location's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which remain unchanged. The method uses stochastic solar-weighted coefficients to take into account solar-energy variability, and demonstrates its versatility through its ability to be seamlessly combined with other conventional quadrature methods. The performance of this novel approach was tested using data from a realistic solar dataset and compared to the standard Gaussian quadrature method, and the results indicate significant performance improvements, with up to 20 times faster processing times and a 10 percent reduction in computation errors.

The curvature formed by the Hessian-Gauss matrix plays a critical role in accelerating optimization algorithms, enabling more efficient exploration of the parameter space via Newton's direction. Despite being computationally expensive to compute, recent advancements have made curvature information more accessible, particularly in reinforcement learning and computer vision, where selecting a low-rank approximation significantly reduces computational costs. However, existing methods often rely on heuristic search techniques, such as random projection, to identify this low-rank structure. In this research, we propose a new approach, ViViT, for automatically selecting an optimal low-rank structure, and demonstrate the method's effectiveness by integrating it with variational inference to train latent Gaussian processes. ViViT's success is validated through experimentation on a variety of real-world and simulated environments, where it consistently enhances performance by providing more accurate representations of the curvature.

Our study provides quantitative evidence that the gender-assignment rules prevalent in languages such as Spanish, where inanimate objects are randomly categorized into male or female genders, result in consistent gender associations within Gender-Representation-Layers (GRS) trained on such languages. These associations reflect the linguistic rules governing gender usage and significantly impact the classification of inanimate objects due to their ambiguous gender-assignment. This phenomenon is demonstrated to be dependent on the model's internal representation of gender and the specific token being classified.

Let $\Gamma = \langle T \rangle$ be a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb{Z})$ with $d \geq 2$ irreducibility and let $B(r) \subset \mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb{Z})$ be a ball of radius $r \geq 0$ centered at the identity element. The maximum growth rate of a group $\Gamma$ is defined as $\mu(\Gamma) = \limsup_{r \to \infty} \frac{\sqrt[r]{B(r)} }{r}$. The goal of this study is to identify the optimal upper bound for the maximum growth rate of any group $\Gamma$ in terms of its irreducibility degree $d$ and its generating set's spectral properties $M(T)$. The method involves applying the Fourier transform to the characteristic function of the ball $B(r)$, specifically utilizing $B(-r)$, to establish a new bound on the growth rate by combining the Deligne bound on $\Gamma \backslash \mathbb{P}^{d-1}(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ with $p \leq 2r$ and Chen's Chinese remainder theorem. The developed bound is applied to specific subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb{Z})$ and a new stiffness bound for the growth rate of the unimodular group $SU_d(\mathbb{Z

Estimating an object's position on a scene-level image is crucial for various computer vision applications, with the potential to be used in conjunction with vision-based manipulation techniques. However, accurately determining an object's pose is complicated by the fact that position alone is often insufficient as it does not provide information about which specific object is being targeted. This problem is further complicated by the lack of labeled datasets, analysis of existing datasets, and limitations of current approaches. This work presents a new approach that tackles the challenge of estimating an object's pose without requiring additional data or annotations. This method relies solely on RGB images and demonstrates improved accuracy over the state-of-the-art methods for estimating an object's pose.

Traffic forecasting, a vital component for intelligent transportation systems, is particularly challenging due to its data scarcity and irregularities.
Existing methods, however, often require a large amount of continuous data, limiting their applicability.
To address this issue, this paper introduces novel sparse traffic forecasting methods that build on the principle of similar data patterns.
First, a method utilizing nearest neighbor models is proposed, where user profiles are created to represent the traffic data and a model is trained using a graph neural network.
To improve training efficiency, a graph-based attention mechanism is introduced to introduce user similarities.
Second, a method combining local and remote strategies is introduced, allowing the model to learn from both similar and directly related data.
To accelerate training, a memory bank is proposed to store user profiles and enable rapid user similarity comparisons.
Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches and enabling efficient training.

In the field of graph-based machine learning, variational graph autoencoders (VACAs) have become a significant focus.
VACAs, a distinct form of VAE, learn by recreating the structure of an underlying latent graph, based on observed data.
Unlike other VAE models, VACAs' research has been confined to a "reconstructive" strategy that incorporates the variational objective by utilizing observed data to predict unobserved graph connections.
This paper broadens VACAs to support a more general approach by introducing a directed edge between the VAE's inference and generative components.
Our new framework enables researchers to address both interventional and counterfactual inquiries without relying on a specific distribution over a graph's edge connections.
To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we applied the VAEs to real-world problems, such as analyzing gene expression, predicting protein interactions, and discovering subgraphs within social media networks, to demonstrate the advantages of our method.

We present the initial results of observations made with the REALTA, a specialized hardware designed for real-time monitoring of celestial radio signals. This new hardware is integrated into the LOFAR station at Markhill to enhance the station's capability in fast transient monitoring. LOFAR's data is combined with data from four additional LOFAR stations to form an international array with an extensive range of 100 MHz to 160 MHz. This paper showcases the capabilities of REALTA using a variety of astronomical sources, including observations of Jupiter's strong radio emissions, an imaging of the Vela pulsar, and detections of fast radio bursts from CHIME, as well as continuous monitoring of blazors.

Researchers exploring photonics based on metasurfaces and metamaterials discover novel phenomena and uncover fundamental principles with the incorporation of machine learning. The adoption of machine learning in metasurface design leads to advancements in clever metasurfaces, which utilize computational methods and algorithms. Our review examines the most recent developments in this field, with the objective of inspiring and guiding a more rigorous and deep understanding of machine learning and metasurfaces for the community.

Understanding why certain films become blockbusters is crucial for filmmakers, producers, and distributors. A comprehensive dataset containing information on 18,344 films released between 1950 and 2019 is compiled using the OMDb API. A key finding is that films released in the color format have a 10% higher revenue compared to those released in black and white. In contrast, films made in black and white experience a 12% revenue loss post-release. These discoveries emphasize the significance of pre-release information in a film's commercial success, surpassing predictions based on past attributes.

In power systems, the interplay between voltage stability and frequency stability is intricate and interdependent. Conventional frequency control methods, designed to maintain frequency stability, can inadvertently exacerbate voltage dynamics' instability. A key contributor to this issue is the interaction between fast-acting frequency controls and slow-frequency dynamics of renewable energy sources. A crucial element in this interaction is the active power setpoint, which is automatically adjusted in response to frequency deviations. Surprisingly, it is shown that replacing this setpoint with a slower, operator-controlled frequency feedback can significantly improve the system's dynamic performance. To further investigate and analyze these effects, a new method for assessing the impact of frequency control on voltage dynamics and vice versa has been developed. This method leverages the concept of causal influence, which quantifies the influence of one system's dynamics on the other. An illustrative case study demonstrates the proposed findings and analysis method in action.

Cyber-physical networks are complex systems consisting of interconnected cyber entities and system components, interacting with each other through information exchange cycles. To enhance safety, control, and efficiency in these networks, intelligent agents are added to the central systems, creating a new class of intelligent cyber-physical networks. These networks differ from traditional networks, which focus primarily on safety and efficiency through feedback control. By incorporating intelligent agents, NPNS enable adaptive behavior, prioritizing safety as a prerequisite for efficiency. However, introducing these agents poses risks to the stability of existing systems. To study the impact of intelligent agents on cyber-physical networks, a new research field, intelligent control of NPNS, is emerging. We outline its fundamental challenges and provide example problems and solutions, as well as future directions in this area.

A novel approach has been developed to model the inverse external Compton scattering process that generates observed UV/X-ray emissions in blazar energy spectra. Our simulation tool, MAPPIES, is designed to calculate the time-varying partial polarization of the Compton-scattered photons resulting from interactions between relativistic particles and external radiation fields. Our analysis uses MAPPIES to examine time-varying polarization patterns in four distinct blazars, including 3C 273, 3C 279, M87, and BL Lac. We discovered that our Compton-scattering model can effectively replicate the observed UV/X-ray excess, whereas traditional single-temperature synchrotron models are insufficient. Our results indicate that distinct Compton components are required to replicate the time-varying polarization patterns, with polarization planes that are not aligned. Our comptonized photons exhibit evolutionary characteristics, exhibiting minimal polarization during outbursts and higher polarization during quiescent periods.

We introduce a strategy for resolving complex landscape problems by identifying and eliminating redundant and unhelpful complexities, an approach anecdotally referred to as "the curse of dimensionality." By applying statistical analysis techniques like the Wilson score, we prioritize regions worthy of exploration in the parameter space, effectively reducing the problem's complexity and making it more tractable for optimization algorithms like reinforcement learning. Furthermore, our method enables analytic extension of the objective function, enabling reinforcement learning algorithms to gain insights and explore rather than merely sample, leading to improved results, especially in high-dimensional landscapes. We also provide theoretical justification for this approach by deriving bounds on the confidence interval, thus validating its feasibility.

A research study examines how to identify pure symmetric states using a method that can be applied in real-time. It involves utilizing minimal information from each measurement to make a binary decision, only recording 'continue' or 'stop' and, when measurement results are gathered once the 'stop' decision is made. This method's performance is assessed through its ability to minimize continuing periods without compromising the decision-making accuracy. It has been found that the method consistently achieves near-perfect decision accuracy across long measurement periods and, therefore, its average continuing duration represents the performance metric of interest. By analyzing the method's properties through existing mathematical theories, it is demonstrated that this decision-making approach, together with its average continuing duration, can be precisely determined for two types of symmetric states representing single photons or opposite circular polarizations.

Baryon creation through the quantized fragmentation of QCD strings is a key process responsible for the production of non-strange baryons, such as protons and neutrons, during the fragmentation of strings in a quantum framework. Baryon number conservation is maintained by attaching quark domains to antiblonons, resulting in the formation of loops that convert into mesons. The process begins with helical strings, resulting in loops that break into mesons, but when ends are fixed in antiblonons, they transform into tubes, allowing for the emergence of non-strange baryons. This mechanism aligns with the observed patterns of particle production at a meson peak level and can account for the significantly higher rates of proton and neutron production in comparison to kaons.

The global solar magnetic dynamo naturally produces periodic reversals every ~11 years and switches between north and south magnetic polarity configurations. To understand these cycles and identify the driving mechanisms, researchers have proposed multiple theories and methods for investigation. One key approach involves analyzing variations in north-south helioseismic travel times. To assess these fluctuations' impact, we investigated the contribution of active region currents to travel time measurements, focusing on the role of currents within active regions and their effects on the data. Analysis revealed that active region currents have a negligible impact, with calculated variations in travel times being minimal compared to observation-based estimates.

In the context of inflationary cosmology, primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) are considered as dark energy candidates and candidates for seeding black holes.  When a single tensor mode in the background cosmology is excited by a PMF, it generates gravitational waves (GWs) with a distinct spectrum characterized by multiple peaks.  These PEVs have negligible impact on the cosmic background radiation, but leave an imprint on GW.  Detailed analysis of GW spectra reveals that some peaks fall within the frequency range of the Pulsar Timing Array.  This suggests that GWs generated by PMFs can be detected within the specified frequency range.  To achieve detection, two conditions must be met:  1.  The Hubble parameter must satisfy $H_0 \lesssim 1.04 \times 10^{-29} h^{-1} \mathrm{GeV}$ at the time of evaluation.  2.  The Peccei-Quinn scale must be in the range $10^{10}-10^{12}$ GeV.

Light field data has significant potential for storage and transmission due to its ability to enhance downstream tasks, but its efficient encoding remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce PRISM, an advanced encoder that effectively balances rate-distortion trade-offs. Our model, which learns from data, replicates the light field composition and motion patterns commonly encountered in real-world applications. To address existing compressors' shortcomings, PRISM incorporates specific enhancements such as adaptive block processing, advanced color transformation, and efficient block data transformation using hidden Markov models. Furthermore, PRISM's novel design, which combines 3D light slice compression with a motion-based residual model, enables efficient exploitation of light field characteristics. Our experimental results demonstrate PRISM's superiority over state-of-the-art compressors.

In cross-lingual information retrieval, a query in one language is translated into another to retrieve relevant documents from a multi-language document collection. Although end-to-end neural models have achieved notable progress, they often suffer from poor retrieval performance due to high computational and data requirements. In contrast, traditional machine translation models and vector store search offer reliable performance for cross-lingual retrieval. We introduce an innovative, two-stage pipeline that combines the strengths of interactive and non-interactive models, thereby achieving improved performance with a relatively simple setup. This new pipeline demonstrates state-of-the-art performance with efficient computation and training times, while also showing the benefits of using both interactive and non-interactive models for cross-lingual information retrieval.

This study aimed to develop design-based techniques for accurate area estimation in resource-constrained environments such as those found in low-income countries. A proposed approach combines multiple models to effectively incorporate complex data available at administrative levels, reducing confidence intervals by up to 25% when accounting for design effects at the administrative level. When applicable, a second stage can be introduced where specific administrative units are sampled using available covariates. A novel regression tree algorithm, which incorporates administrative area boundaries as input covariates, was developed. This method's performance was tested using two low-income countries, Burkina Faso and Tanzania, and it was found that the proposed approach showed a significant reduction in error rates and was able to utilize data more effectively across various data types and administrative boundaries compared to traditional methods.

This study explores the application of quantum information in the quantum version of the Kelly criterion. By utilizing quantum information concepts, the quantum master equation was developed to model the logarithmic wealth equation. The quantum counterpart of the wager was represented as a von Neumann measurement, and according to the quantum version of the Kelly criterion, the optimal quantum wager was determined. A proposed framework for quantum wealth based on quantum coherent states was demonstrated to display non-classical behavior in its corresponding quantum counterpart.

Recent advancements in 2D material synthesis have led to the creation of numerous exciting 2D materials, including the recently developed MA$_2$Z$_4$ family (where M is either Mo, W, or Ti; A is either Si, Ge; and Z is N, P, or As).
